lead: Naive Bayes classifier predicts a class by multiplying a prior probability with the likelihood of each feature assuming the features are independent. It is fast, works well with text and sensor data, and is used in spam filters, sentiment analysis, and medical diagnosis.
prereq: You need: Bayes theorem and MAP from Chapter 3.2.

blocks.text: Given a feature vector X = (x₁, x₂, …, xₙ) and a set of classes C₁ … Cₖ, we want the posterior probability P(Cⱼ|X). Bayes theorem gives P(Cⱼ|X) = P(Cⱼ)·P(X|Cⱼ) / P(X).
The naïve assumption says the features are conditionally independent given the class. Therefore P(X|Cⱼ) = ∏_{i=1}^{n} P(xᵢ|Cⱼ).

blocks.where: P(Cⱼ) is the prior probability of class Cⱼ; P(xᵢ|Cⱼ) is the likelihood of feature xᵢ under class Cⱼ; P(X) is a normalising constant common to all classes.

blocks.text: Because P(X) is the same for every class, we can compare the numerators only. The predicted class is argmax_{Cⱼ} P(Cⱼ)·∏ P(xᵢ|Cⱼ).

items: Fast to train – only count frequencies.

Works with high‑dimensional data – the product can be computed in log space. Computing log probabilities avoids numerical underflow because the product of many small numbers becomes a sum of negative logs, which stays within floating‑point range.
Often surprisingly accurate despite the independence assumption.

blocks.text: Training a multinomial Naive Bayes model for text is a matter of counting word occurrences in each class.

items: Count total documents in each class → N_{Cⱼ}.
Count total word tokens in each class → N_{Cⱼ}^{tot}.
For each word w, count occurrences in class Cⱼ → N_{w,Cⱼ}.

blocks.where: α is the Laplace smoothing constant (usually 1); V is the vocabulary size; N_{w,Cⱼ} is the count of word w in class Cⱼ; N_{Cⱼ}^{tot} is the total word count in class Cⱼ.

blocks.text: Without smoothing, a word unseen in a class gives probability zero and forces the whole product to zero. Adding α > 0 avoids this problem.

items: Choose α by cross‑validation if data are scarce.

blocks.text: When features are continuous, we replace the discrete likelihood with a Gaussian density.

blocks.where: μ_{Cⱼ} and σ_{Cⱼ}² are the mean and variance of feature xᵢ computed over the training samples that belong to class Cⱼ.

blocks.text: Multinomial NB is best for word count vectors. Bernoulli NB treats each word as a binary feature (present / absent).

items: Scaling numeric features before using Gaussian NB is optional; do it when features have very different units or for numerical stability.
Remove stop‑words and apply stemming for text data.
Use log probabilities to avoid underflow: compute log P(C) + Σ log P(xᵢ|C).

blocks.text: Naive Bayes is a baseline for many competitions. It is also used in real‑time systems because classification is O(number of features).

examples.question: A spam filter uses a multinomial Naive Bayes model. The vocabulary consists of the words "free" and "win" only (V = 2). In the training set, spam messages contain 30 occurrences of "free" and 20 of "win" out of a total of 100 word tokens. Ham messages contain 5 occurrences of "free" and 2 of "win" out of a total of 200 word tokens. Using Laplace smoothing with α = 1, compute the posterior probability that a new message containing both words (one occurrence each) is spam.
steps: Compute prior probabilities based on document counts:
Compute smoothed likelihoods for each word:
examples.answer: The posterior probability that the message is spam is about 0.986 (98.6%).
examples.check:
import math
prior_spam = 40/120
prior_ham = 80/120
P_free_spam = (30+1)/(100+2)
P_win_spam = (20+1)/(100+2)
P_free_ham = (5+1)/(200+2)
P_win_ham = (2+1)/(200+2)
score_spam = prior_spam * P_free_spam * P_win_spam
score_ham = prior_ham * P_free_ham * P_win_ham
post_spam = score_spam / (score_spam + score_ham)
print(round(post_spam,3))

traps: Forgetting Laplace smoothing makes the probability of an unseen word zero, turning the whole product to zero.
Dividing by the total number of words instead of the total word tokens in the class gives wrong likelihoods.
Using raw probabilities instead of log probabilities can cause underflow for long messages.
Mixing up P(C) with P(X) leads to forgetting the normalisation step; the denominator P(X) cancels only when comparing classes.

quiz.q: What does the ‘naïve’ part of Naive Bayes refer to?
quiz.a: The assumption that all features are conditionally independent given the class.

quiz.q: Explain why Laplace smoothing is needed in a multinomial Naive Bayes model.
quiz.a: It adds a small count α to every word‑class pair, preventing zero probabilities for words not seen in training. This avoids the product becoming zero and improves generalisation.

quiz.q: Given a binary feature that is true in 8 out of 20 positive examples and false in 2 out of 20 negative examples, compute the likelihoods P(feature|positive) and P(feature|negative) with α = 1 and V = 2.

A document contains three words: "free", "win", "free". Using the likelihoods from the example (P(free|spam)=0.3039, P(win|spam)=0.2059, P(free|ham)=0.0297, P(win|ham)=0.0149) and priors from the example, compute the unnormalised spam score.
quiz.a: Count: free appears twice, win once. Score_spam = P(spam)·P(free|spam)²·P(win|spam) = 0.3333·0.3039²·0.2059 ≈ 0.0067.

quiz.q: Compare Gaussian Naive Bayes and Multinomial Naive Bayes. When would you choose each?
quiz.a: Gaussian NB models continuous numeric features with a normal distribution; use it for sensor readings, age, etc. Multinomial NB models discrete count data such as word frequencies; use it for text classification, document tagging, etc.

quiz.q: Why is it safe to ignore the denominator P(X) when selecting the most probable class?
quiz.a: P(X) is the same for every class, so it does not affect the relative ordering of posterior probabilities.

beyond: Not for the exam. Naive Bayes is being extended with hierarchical priors for large‑scale language models. Researchers combine it with word embeddings to capture some dependence between words. In industry, it powers real‑time fraud detection where speed is critical. Future study can look at Bayesian networks for structured data or deep generative models that relax the independence assumption.
